title: 1981 Pushkin Tu-104 crash
summary: Tupolev Tu-104A aircraft crashed during takeoff from Pushkin Airport near Leningrad on 7 February 1981, killing all 50 on board. After rotation, the aircraft pitched up beyond normal takeoff attitude. Eight seconds after liftoff at 50 m altitude, the Tu-104 stalled and entered a right bank, striking the ground 20 m from the departure end of the runway. The investigation revealed the aircraft was improperly loaded with military officers not complying with seating assignments and large rolls of printing paper loaded in the cargo hold. The cargo rolled rearward during takeoff acceleration, shifting the center of gravity aft of acceptable limits, reducing pitch stability and making nose-down control impossible.
probable_cause: The crew allowed the aircraft to be improperly loaded. Military officers did not comply with seating assignments and pressured the crew to fly in an unsafely loaded aircraft. Large rolls of printing paper rolled rearward during takeoff acceleration, causing the center of gravity to shift aft of acceptable limits, reducing aircraft pitch stability.

title: Austral Líneas Aéreas 901
summary: Flight 901 on approach to Buenos Aires encountered severe thunderstorms with heavy rain and winds. After aborting the first landing attempt, the crew conducted a go-around and second approach. Despite observing cumulonimbus clouds, the crew turned toward the river and then northward directly into the center of the storm. The aircraft lost control and crashed into the Río de la Plata, killing all 31 on board.
probable_cause: Loss of control and impact against water due to pilot error in evaluating meteorological conditions while crossing through the zone of influence of an extremely violent cumulonimbus.

title: Aeroflot 498
summary: Aeroflot Flight 498, an Ilyushin Il-14M, departed Severomuysk on June 14, 1981 for Baikal with a planned stop at Nizhneangarsk but was rerouted due to poor weather. Operating with visibility of only 5 kilometers in rain and wind, the ARP-6 navigation data finder was unstable and the aircraft deviated 32 kilometers right of course. While descending from 3,600 to 2,700 meters, the crew violated procedures by calling the wrong air tower, failed to report location, and mistook Holy Nose Peninsula for the airfield. The aircraft descended below safe altitude and crashed into a mountainside at 1,300 meters, killing all 48 aboard.

title: 1981 Armenia mid-air collision
summary: A Transporte Aéreo Rioplatense Canadair CL-44 cargo aircraft strayed into Soviet airspace over Armenia while returning from Tehran to Larnaca on 18 July 1981. Soviet air defense scrambled a Sukhoi Su-15 fighter to intercept. After the CL-44 crew failed to respond to radio calls and visual signals, the Su-15 pilot collided with the CL-44's tail. The three Argentine crew and passenger died; the Soviet pilot ejected successfully.
probable_cause: The CL-44 deviated off course and strayed into Soviet airspace in violation of international boundaries. The crew failed to respond to intercept signals from the Soviet fighter pilot. The collision that followed may have been intentional or the result of misjudgment by the Soviet pilot. The aircraft was engaged in prohibited arms transport from Israel to Iran.

title: Somali Airlines 40
summary: Somali Airlines Flight 40 crashed a few minutes after takeoff from Mogadishu on 20 July 1981. According to the Aviation Safety Network, the aircraft entered a spiral dive after encountering strong vertical gusts, leading to separation of its right wing. The crew had returned to Mogadishu for repairs due to an unspecified malfunction before departing again. A preliminary investigation suggested a technical fault, though the specific cause was not definitively established.

title: 1981 Bristow Helicopters Westland Wessex crash
summary: A Westland Wessex 60 operated by Bristow Helicopters transporting 11 gas workers from Leman field platforms to Bacton experienced loss of power to the main rotor gearbox. The helicopter went out of control during autorotation and crashed into the North Sea. All 13 people on board died. The wreck was beyond recovery by the time salvage operations started, and there was insufficient evidence to determine the cause of the power loss or loss of control.

title: Far Eastern Air Transport 103
summary: The Boeing 737 had lost cabin pressure twice: once on August 5 and again on takeoff August 22 before the flight was aborted. After repairs, the aircraft departed again and 14 minutes into climb at 18,000 feet it suffered explosive decompression and disintegrated. An investigation concluded severe corrosion from numerous pressurization cycles caused a pressure-hull rupture. Wreckage was scattered over a 4-mile area in multiple townships.

The starboard wing separated in the intense vortices and the aircraft spun into the ground near Moerdijk, killing all seventeen occupants.

title: Aeroflot 3603
summary: Aeroflot Flight 3603, a Tupolev Tu-154 carrying approximately 102 passengers and crew, departed Krasnoyarsk for Norilsk on November 17, 1981. The aircraft was 5,000 lb above calculated weight with center of gravity beyond the forward limit, causing a nose-heavy condition. During approach in dark conditions with low overcast at 400 feet, the aircraft descended below the glide path. After attempting a go-around, the aircraft struck terrain 1,500 feet short of the runway. Of 167 aboard, 99 were killed and 68 survived.
probable_cause: The cause of the accident was loss of longitudinal control at the final stage of landing due to forward alignment position, reduced elevator effectiveness at high deflection angles, and late recognition of the emergency situation by the crew.

factors.evidence: The aircraft was about 5,000 lb above its calculated weight and its center of gravity was beyond the forward limit for the type.

Nominal load was calculated based on incorrect standard weights; four passengers were not issued coupons, adding unaccounted small children aboard; actual weight was 685 kg more than indicated in transportation documents.

A significant decrease in elevator margin was revealed during Tu-154B flight tests, compared to the first Tu-154; the front centering limit was changed from 18 to 16.5% of the MAC but this did not compensate for decreased longitudinal control margin.
Crew did not recognize the forward center of gravity condition during loading; no indicator for maximum permissible elevator deviations existed in cockpit.
The nose heavy condition caused Flight 3603 to descend below the glide path as it made its final approach.
The aircraft's longitudinal control was lost when elevator was deflected; the crew decided to go around but it was too late due to low altitude.
Aircraft impacted terrain approximately 1,500 ft short of runway.

events.text: Aircraft began approach to Norilsk Airport in dark conditions with low overcast cloud base of approximately 400 feet.
Captain initiated descent but nose heavy condition caused aircraft to descend below the glide path during final approach.
Captain initiated go-around maneuver and deflected elevator all the way to pitch up to reduce vertical speed.

At speed of 261-263 km/h, longitudinal control was lost; crew lacked sufficient elevator effectiveness due to high deflection angle and forward CG position; aircraft impacted terrain approximately 1,500 ft short of runway.

title: Inex-Adria Aviopromet 1308
summary: Inex-Adria Flight 1308, an MD-82 charter flight with 180 Yugoslavian tourists and crew, crashed into Mont San Petru on 1 December 1981 on its final approach to Ajaccio. The crew, unfamiliar with Ajaccio airport, were in a holding pattern over mountainous terrain while ATC mistakenly believed they were over the sea. Imprecise language between crew and controller, combined with the controller's confusion about the aircraft position, led to a fatal clearance to descend into terrain.
probable_cause: The accident resulted from imprecise language used by the crew and air traffic controller. ATC mistakenly believed that Flight 1308 was out of its holding pattern and located over the sea, when in reality the aircraft was located 15 km inland over the mountainous terrain of Corsica. The crew, unfamiliar with the airport and its vicinity, descended on ATC clearance into terrain. The Ajaccio airport lacked radar to detect the conflict.
